newsitem.title: USA: Cuba's human rights record worsened, U.S. says.
newsitem.headline: Cuba's human rights record worsened, U.S. says.

text.p: The human rights record of communist-ruled Cuba, over which the United States and its allies are at odds, worsened last year and suppression of dissent increased, the U.S. State Department said on Thursday.

In its annual survey of individual rights around the world, the department branded Cuba a "totalitarian anachronism" under the iron grip of President Fidel Castro, a thorn in the side of nine U.S. presidents since he deposed a U.S.-backed government in 1959.

"The government's human rights record worsened in 1996," the report said. It cited, among other things, a crackdown on an umbrella group of pro-democracy forces, the shooting down on Feb. 24 of two small U.S. civilian airplanes in international airspace and increased reports of deaths due to excessive use of force by police.

The State Department also cited further curbs on the distribution of foreign publications, antagonism to foreign government criticism of human rights practices, restrictions on foreign contacts with human rights activists and expulsions of visiting foreign journalists.

"The authorities continued routinely to harass, threaten, arbitrarily arrrest, detain, imprison, defame, and physically attack human rights advocates and members of independent professional associations," the department said.

The report on Cuba, one of 193 countries surveyed by the department, has broad implications because of disputes over a U.S. law enacted last year that would let U.S. citizens sue some foreign companies that do business in Cuba.

President Bill Clinton on Jan. 3 extended a delay in implementation of a provision of the Helms-Burton act, saying he would keep on delaying it as long as U.S. allies continued a stepped-up effort "to promote a transition to democracy in Cuba."
The provision would let U.S. citizens, including Cubans who were naturalised, sue foreign firms that profit from properties confiscated by Cuba after its 1959 revolution.
The law, enacted last March, enraged Europeans, Canadians and Mexicans who argued that the United States was trying to impose its anti-Cuba trade legislation.
Several countries have taken steps to counter Helms-Burton, named after its Republican sponsors in Congress.

On Tuesday, Sir Leon Brittan, vice president of the European Commission, said after meeting the new U.S. Secretary of State, Madeleine Albright, that the European Union would continue to challenge Helms-Burton at the World Trade Organisation until it was scrapped or amended.

Clinton, seeking to calm tensions, first suspended the lawsuit provision in July for six months. He named a special envoy to work with U.S. allies and anti-Castro Cuban-Americans on trying to bring democracy to Cuba.
After consultations with the envoy, Stuart Eizenstat, members of the European Union agreed in December to press Cuba further on human rights and democracy.
Clinton objected to key parts of Helms-Burton but signed it after Cuba shot down two civilian aircraft piloted by anti-Castro activists, killing all four people aboard.

The State Department report endorsed a finding by the human rights group Amnesty International that Cuba had shifted tactics in suppressing dissent. Rather than arresting dissidents and bringing them to trial, the government now was tending to force them into exile, Amnesty said.
The State Department said Cuba applied this tactic to dozens of members of Concilio Cubano, a pro-democracy umbrella movement of more than 130 groups founded in 1995.
